title: India Routes $11.6B in Orders to Domestic Industry as South Korea's Record Budget Puts Drones First; Iran Used Claude AI to Target US Navy, Anthropic Says
subhead: New Delhi approved $11.6 billion in procurement with roughly 98% sourced domestically, Seoul unveiled a record $53.9 billion budget built around drones as the main fighting vehicle, and Anthropic disclosed Iranian actors used its Claude AI to compile targeting on US Navy forces. Together they mark a day when Asian defense-industrial autonomy and AI-enabled targeting both moved decisively.

sections.heading: India Approves $11.6B in Orders, ~98% Domestic
sections.body:
India's Defense Acquisition Council, chaired by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, granted in-principle approval to roughly $11.6 billion in military hardware with the government aiming to source about 98% from Indian industry, Defense News reports. The approvals cover all three services — CBRN reconnaissance vehicles, mine-laying and high-mobility vehicles for the Army; surveillance radars and domestically designed marine gas turbines for the Navy; and a ground-based multi-purpose jammer plus unspecified fighter, transport and helicopter upgrades for the Air Force.

The ministry says roughly 65% of India's military hardware is now produced domestically, a reversal from a decade ago when about two-thirds was imported. Nearly a quarter of the roughly $20 billion in defense equipment produced in fiscal 2025-26 came from private firms, and New Delhi is pushing private industry's share toward 50%. Funds come from $86 billion annual defense budget. Defense News notes observers caution that drone and other equipment still relies on imported sensors and avionics, and India continues to depend on foreign suppliers for fighter jets.
sections.whyItMatters: India is deliberately converting procurement into industrial policy — the private-sector share of a self-sufficiency drive aimed at cutting strategic exposure to foreign suppliers. The caveat matters: domestic assembly without control of sensors, chips and engines still leaves critical dependence, and the marine gas-turbine and fighter-engine gaps are the hardest to close.

sections.heading: Anthropic: Iranian Actors Used Claude to Target US Navy
sections.body:
A Anthropic report covering December 2025 to August 2026 found Iranian bad actors used the company's publicly accessible Claude model to compile 'targeting handbooks' against US Navy forces in the Middle East, according to Military Times. The threat actor used open-source information — public military photos of service members, ship and aircraft transponder codes, commercial satellite-imagery query scripts and websites tracking Navy movements — to identify and track positions, and to probe weaknesses in shipboard systems.

Anthropic said it banned the account, added safeguards and shared findings with government agencies. The same report detailed a Yemeni cell that used Claude to develop targeting software for guided missiles. Separately, researchers Jacob Coxon resigned from both Anthropic and OpenAI over ethics concerns, and the Pentagon severed ties with the platform earlier this year over terms about mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, according to Military Times.
sections.whyItMatters: This documents a concrete shift: adversaries are not just buying commercial AI — they are using accessible frontier models as open-source-intelligence analysis engines to build targeting products. It puts commercial AI firms in the middle of intelligence contest, and highlights the asymmetry where US forces cannot always use the same models freely while adversaries can.

sections.heading: South Korea's Record Budget Puts Drones at Center of Military
sections.body:
South Korea's defense budget will rise 8.2% to KRW 73.28 trillion (~$53.9 billion), a record, after the government announced the plan on Sept. 3, Defense News reports from the KADEX-run defence trade context. The Ministry of National Defense said it will 'use drones as the main fighting vehicle for our military,' with unmanned spending up almost 20%. Seoul plans drone swarms, reconnaissance drones, loitering munitions and a counter-drone system, and will train half a million 'drone warriors'.

Funding for the KF-21 Boramae fighter nearly triples to KRW 3.3 trillion as first production jets are built; the L-SAM long-range air defense and MUAV medium-altitude drones are named big-ticket items, with nearly KRW 100 billion for nuclear-powered submarines. Funding to prepare for the wartime OPCON transfer from the US is up 35%, targeting completion by 2029. Defense News frames the spending against North Korea, China and Russia concerns and President Trump's August order scaling back US-South Korean drills.
sections.whyItMatters: Seoul is answering an aging-recruit pool and a receding US exercise footprint with a high-tech, unmanned-centric force — drones redefined from a supporting weapon to the primary fighting vehicle, with a half-million-strong trained operator base as the manpower answer to conscription shortfalls.

sections.heading: US Military Relearns How to Hide as Iranian Strikes Expose Base Vulnerability
sections.body:
Iranian attacks on US bases across the Middle East have pushed the Army's Combined Arms Command to overhaul doctrine on concealment, Military Times reports. 'Hiding in plain sight has become an imperative on the modern battlefield,' Lt. Gen. James P. Isenhower told a Thursday Pentagon briefing, emphasizing dispersal and shrinking command posts against long-range fires and drones.

The reporting details the emerging scale of damage: an Iranian strike on NSA Bahrain on Feb. 28, which the Wall Street Journal estimated at roughly $400 million, with acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao saying Iran 'blew the hell out of Bahrain.' Three US soldiers died in a July strike at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, and six in a March drone strike at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait. Separately, Iran's attack on the Jordan base this week damaged one A-10 and eight F-15s, per a US official cited by Defense News.
sections.whyItMatters: A force that spent two decades not worrying about precision fires is re-learning Cold War-era dispersal as a survival skill. The disclosed Bahrain damage shows the cost of the old 'sprawling, easy-to-find' footprint, and doctrine is now being rewritten around concealment as a core competency.

sections.heading: Ukrainian Industry Races Jet-Powered Interceptors Against Russian Jet Drones
sections.body:
At the MSPO defense show in Kielce, Poland, Ukrainian firms displayed a new generation of interceptors aimed at Russia's shift to jet-powered drones, Defense News reports. General Cherry is developing a kinetic booster version of its Bullet interceptor targeting ~450 km/h with heat-resistant materials; Grim Tech aims for 500-700 km/h with a jet-powered interceptor planned by late October.

A Grim Tech manager told Defense News that Russia 'uses almost only jet-powered Shaheds to attack Kyiv' and that earlier interceptor generations hit around 90% against older drones. BlueBird Tech is building an air-defense interceptor designed to cost less than the targets it destroys, with R&D cycles measured in weeks. The push comes as Ukraine readies for a potential lifting of its arms-export embargo that would let firms sell abroad.
sections.whyItMatters: The economics are explicit — interceptors must cost less than the munitions they catch for counter-drone defense to scale. Ukraine's week-scale R&D cycles and price-constrained design philosophy are producing a template the broader industry is watching, with export potential once the embargo lifts.

sections.heading: US Navy Next-Gen Fighter Decision Imminent; Anduril Doubles Down on Poland
sections.body:
Two procurement signals round out the day. Sources told Defense News the US Navy's next-generation fighter decision is expected to be unveiled soon — a program that will define the service's sixth-generation air combat direction. Separately, Anduril is pitching two autonomous aircraft types to accompany Poland's planned F-35 and Apache fleets, stepping up its European expansion at the same MSPO event.

On the ongoing Gulf and China files: Saudi Arabia's request for US military help against the Houthis and China's J-10CE export drive (with Uzbekistan confirmed as second operator) both continued as covered in recent briefs; neither materially advanced since yesterday.
sections.whyItMatters: The Navy fighter decision resets US air-power procurement at a moment when sixth-gen programs are crowding budgets, while Anduril's Poland push shows US defense-technology firms treating Eastern Europe — not just Washington — as the growth market.

bottomLine: The day's center of gravity was Asian defense-industrialism: India routed ~$11.6 billion in new orders to domestic industry on a 98% self-sourcing target, and South Korea's record $53.9 billion budget made drones the primary fighting vehicle and trained a half-million strong operator base. In parallel, Anthropic's disclosure that Iranian actors used its Claude model to compile targeting against US Navy forces marks the first mainstream documentation of an adversary weaponizing a commercial frontier model for open-source targeting. The US military's own response — relearning concealment after tens of billions in Iranian damage to Gulf bases — and Ukraine's price-driven interceptor race round out a day where both the buyers of weapons and the tools of targeting are being redefined.
sources: Defense News, Military Times, Wall Street Journal (via Military Times), Anthropic (via Military Times)
